children.text: On Baguio's east side, Wright Park and The Mansion, the president's summer residence, face each other across a long pine-lined pool. Built in
, The Mansion has been open since
as a free presidential museum, and the park offers pony rides.
Wright Park and The Mansion are two landmarks facing each other across a single road in the Lualhati area, about
3–4 km

east of Burnham Park in downtown Baguio. Walk from the park along the long pool flanked by pine trees and you reach, in turn, The Mansion's wrought-iron gate, a broad lawn and the white, green-roofed building; The Mansion mirrored upside down in the water is counted among Baguio's signature photo views. Locals call the park "Wright Park," and the reflecting pool is widely known as the "Pool of Pines."
The American colonial government built The Mansion as the Governor-General's summer residence, completing it in

. Architect William E. Parsons designed it based on the ideas of Daniel Burnham, who drew up Baguio's city plan, and William Cameron Forbes, who later became Governor-General, is said to have named it after his family's home in Massachusetts. In
the Second Philippine Legislature held a special session here, and from the Commonwealth period on it became the official summer residence of the President of the Philippines, as it remains today.
Heavily damaged by bombing in World War II, the building was rebuilt in

with added guest rooms and conference spaces. Afterward it hosted the second session of the UN Economic Commission for Asia and the Far East (ECAFE), the second session of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) in
, and in
the Baguio Conference of Southeast Asian leaders convened by President Elpidio Quirino. The National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) declared it a National Historical Landmark on
January 16, 2009
, and after a major renovation The Mansion opened to the public on
September 8, 2024
as the Presidential Museum, displaying memorabilia and paintings of past presidents.
Wright Park is a wooded park named after Luke E. Wright, Governor-General of the Philippines in

, and was laid out as a recreation area during the American colonial period. Pine and agoho (casuarina) trees line both sides of the pool, and past the wooden pergola at the pool's west end, a long stone stairway leads down to the riding area where you can rent ponies. The horses are led by "pony boys," many of them Ibaloi. Since neither the park nor the museum charges admission, it makes a fitting half-day outing for history lovers, families who want a pony ride with their kids and photographers alike.

blocks.title: Photograph The Mansion in the Pool of Pines

children.text: From the west end of the pool, looking toward the gate, you see the gate and The Mansion reflected upside down on the water. Early morning, when the air is still and crowds are thin, is best, and benches along the paved walkways on both sides of the pool make for an easy stroll.
Rooms of the residence have been turned into galleries showing memorabilia and paintings of past presidents. Admission is free, and from Tuesday to Sunday groups of up to 20 go in with a guide every
30 minutes
between
and

The wrought-iron gate with its scrollwork is the most photographed gateway in Baguio. A popular story says it was modeled on the main gate of Buckingham Palace, but this has never been confirmed. Read the historical marker on the gate pillar, and frame the lawn with its "THE MANSION" lettering and the building beyond the gate.
At the riding area below the stairs, you ride a pony led by a pony boy around a circular track or along forest paths. There is no official rate card; the going rate is reportedly about
for
30 minutes
, so agree on time and price before you get on.

blocks.title: Wooden pergola and long stone stairway

children.text: At the west end of the pool stands an old pergola built from thick timber posts, which photographs well in the morning sun. A steep stone stairway runs from it down to the riding area, and the view of the pine forest from the top of the steps is worth a look too.

In a small garden near the riding area stands a gold-painted statue of a warrior on horseback. It honors the "Baguio Apaches," a long-standing local fellowship group in Baguio named after the Apache leader Geronimo.

The entrance road on the riding-area side is lined with potted-plant and flower stalls, souvenir shops and strawberry taho vendors. There are also souvenir-photo stalls where you pose with a Saint Bernard or in Igorot traditional costume, charging roughly

Baguio
entry.

From downtown, take a jeepney marked "Mines View" and ask the driver to drop you at Wright Park or in front of The Mansion. The ride takes
10–15 minutes
and costs about

To return, catch a downtown (Plaza)-bound jeepney on the main road in front of the park. Routes and loading points change often, so ask your accommodation first.
From Session Road or Burnham Park, the ride takes
10–15 minutes
without traffic and costs about
on the meter. Always ask the driver to turn the meter on.

Tell the driver "The Mansion" to be dropped at the main gate, or "Wright Park Riding Circle" for the riding-area entrance. Empty taxis are scarce on weekend afternoons, so arrange your ride back early.
From Manila, drive via NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX and climb to Baguio on Marcos Highway, which takes about
4–6 hours
. Kennon Road is often closed for rockfalls or repairs, so check whether it is open first.
The road in front of The Mansion's gate is a no-parking zone, and parking around the park is tight. On weekends it is better to leave your car at your accommodation and come by taxi or jeepney.
From Mines View Park it is about
downhill along the road, about
20–25 minutes
on foot. Some stretches have narrow sidewalks, so a taxi is easier with children or older companions.
The Baguio Botanical Garden is connected by Leonard Wood Road, about
10 minutes
on foot. The pool path in the park is flat, but the stone stairway down to the riding area is steep.
Wright Park and The Mansion's grounds are outdoors, so the weather makes a big difference to your visit. Baguio's average annual temperature is about
, and in the
November–April
dry season the skies are clear and cool, perfect for sharp shots of The Mansion reflected in the pool. In
December
a large Christmas tree goes up in front of The Mansion's gate with a lighting ceremony, drawing more evening strollers, while the whole city gets crowded during the Panagbenga Flower Festival in
February
and Holy Week in
March–April
In the
June–October
rainy season, afternoon showers and thick fog are common, and during heavy rain or typhoons the city temporarily closes parks and attractions. On
August 31, 2026

, bad weather closed Wright Park, The Mansion, Mines View Park and the Botanical Garden all at once. In the rainy season, check the Baguio City Tourism Office's announcements before you set out. That said, the Pool of Pines on a foggy morning has an atmosphere you only get in the wet season.

Pensions and guesthouses are scattered among the pines along Leonard Wood Road, Gibraltar Road and Outlook Drive around the park, so staying here makes it easy to see the pool early in the morning before the crowds arrive. If you want the bus terminal, market and restaurants close at hand, stay downtown around Session Road or Burnham Park and take a
10–15 minute
taxi ride. Rates per night are about
for a guesthouse and about
for a mid-range hotel, rising sharply and selling out early at year-end, during Panagbenga and over Holy Week.
There are hardly any proper restaurants in the park; the stalls on the riding-area entrance road sell little more than snacks such as strawberry taho (about

) and grilled corn. Food and drinks are not allowed inside the museum, so eat before your tour. For meals, head to the restaurants at nearby Camp John Hay or the long-established bakeries and cafés on Session Road, and for gifts, the ube jam and strawberry jam from the Good Shepherd Convent near Mines View are famous. On cool days, warm fare such as Benguet coffee or bulalo, a beef bone-marrow soup, hits the spot.
Museum tours depart every
30 minutes
from
to
, Tuesday to Sunday (with a break around noon). Without a reservation, get a number at the visitor center and go in when a slot opens.
To be sure of a place, book on the
tour reservation page
at least three working days ahead (excluding Mondays and holidays). Groups of more than 20 are split and moved to the next slot, and small parties are combined with other visitors.
The museum asks visitors to avoid sleeveless tops, tank tops and slippers. Children must be at least five years old and accompanied by a parent or guardian.
Inside the museum, photos are allowed only in designated areas and video recording is prohibited. Do not touch the exhibits.
Photos of the gate and lawn can be taken without a tour from
8:00 AM to 5:00 PM
within the designated area. For pool-reflection shots, early morning when the air is still is best.
Agree clearly on time, route and price before riding a pony. Some handlers charge separately when two people take turns on one horse, so ask in advance.
Some park restrooms charge a fee of about
, and the stalls take cash only, so bring small bills and coins.
Tour groups crowd in on weekends from
10:00 AM to 4:00 PM
. Weekday early mornings are the quietest.

The Mansion is still the president's official summer residence. Security staff accompany every tour, and tours can be stopped if safety rules are broken, so do not stray outside the designated areas. Opening hours differ slightly between sources, so check the official announcements before visiting.
During heavy rain or typhoons, the city closes Wright Park and The Mansion temporarily without notice. In the rainy season, check the Baguio City Tourism Office's announcements before setting out.
The riding area smells of horse dung and turns muddy after rain. Wear comfortable shoes, don't stand behind the horses and keep a firm hold of children's hands.
Since

, construction of multipurpose buildings that will house stables and stalls has been under way near the riding area, so some sections may be closed or the horses' waiting area may move. Follow the barriers and signs.
The stone stairway beside the pergola is steep and slippery after rain. Older visitors and strollers should use the level path along the pool.
The road in front of The Mansion is busy and a no-parking zone. Take care crossing, and on crowded days keep your phone and wallet in a bag worn in front.
